column1: # The docstring states the rule outright: "To be equivalent, they must be identical on all
# fields not modified on input by the LRS and identical on other fields, if these fields are
# present in both statements. For example, if an "authority" field is present in only one
# statement, they may still be equivalent."
# 🟢 AND RALPH IS STRICTER THAN THE SPEC, which is worth saying: the comment reads "The LRS
# specification excludes the fields below from equivalency. It was decided to include them
# anyway as their value is inherent to the statements." That is timestamp and version.
# `stored` is LRS-set and ignoring it is correct.
## WHY THE GUARANTEE DOES NOT NARROW — the branch, re-read at statements.py:683-693
# if existing_statements:
#     for existing in existing_statements:
#         if not statements_are_equivalent(statement_as_dict, existing):
#             raise HTTPException(409, "A different statement already exists with the same ID")
#     return                       <-- bare return, BEFORE BACKEND_CLIENT.write
# 🟢 BOTH branches leave the stored bytes untouched:
#   NOT equivalent -> 409, returns before the write is reached.
#   equivalent     -> bare `return`, 204, no write call at all.
# 🟢 So a re-PUT differing ONLY in `authority` is judged equivalent, answers 204, and
# WRITES NOTHING. There is no overwrite. p189's limb 2 anticipated "accepted as equivalent
# and the 409 guarantee has a hole"; the acceptance is real, the hole is not.
# Same shape on POST: _filter_existing_statements (188-210) raises 409 on a non-equivalent
# duplicate id and REMOVES equivalent ids from the write set by dict comprehension.
## 🔴 WHAT IS ACTUALLY HOLED — attribution, and silently
# `authority` is the field recording WHO ASSERTED the statement. Because it is outside the
# comparison:
# 1. 🔴 Two statements with the same id and DIFFERENT asserting authorities are treated as
#    THE SAME STATEMENT. The second is accepted with 204 and DISCARDED.
# 2. 🔴 A client cannot distinguish "your statement was stored" from "your statement was
#    dropped because another authority already claimed that id". Both are 204.
# 3. 🟡 timestamp and version are compared only when present in both, so a statement WITH a
#    timestamp and one WITHOUT are equivalent on that field.
## CONSEQUENCE FOR PATTERN 32
# 🟢 Step 3c stands exactly as p189 repriced it, and the 409 CAN be quoted to a DPO
#   unqualified: the application layer will not mutate a stored statement, on either write path.
# 🔴 What CANNOT be quoted unqualified is "the LRS distinguishes two asserters of the same
#   statement id". It does not. For a trail whose value is WHO decided, the asserting
#   authority is outside the integrity comparison and a conflicting claim is swallowed as a
#   duplicate. 🟢 The fix is cheap and belongs in step 3c: mint statement ids per authority,
#   or reject on authority mismatch at the ingest proxy. Add no weeks; add one guard.
# 🟢 Step 3b (the WORM store) is unaffected and stays mandatory for the OPERATOR adversary,
#   which is p189's split and still holds.
## 🔵 THE CROSS-ARTEFACT FINDING, and it is this pass's trend measured twice
# ralph  — protects the RECORD in code (409, both paths) and leaves ATTRIBUTION outside the
#          comparison (`authority` never compared).
# openedx-mcp — protects the RECORD in its admin (add blocked, change blocked, every field
#          readonly) and leaves ATTRIBUTION deletable (key and user are SET_NULL; the audit
#          log's delete permission is never overridden). See
#          evidence/openedx-mcp-tool-surface.2026-10-14-p190.tsv F2.
# 🔴 Two unrelated codebases, two different languages, two different layers of the stack,
# the same omission: the thing protected is the ROW, and the thing left unprotected is WHO.
# 🟢 p189 named the trend as "nobody protects the durable record of a human decision about a
# learner". p190 sharpens it: the record IS protected in both. The ACTOR is not.
